narrative.documentConcept: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
narrative.text: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol require separate interpretations for PD incidence and treatment after diagnosis. Several cohorts associate caffeine or coffee with lower PD risk, but a large UK Biobank analysis found no overall association and reported genotype heterogeneity; caffeine did not improve motor outcomes in Café-PD. Smoking has an inverse epidemiologic association, with supportive but assumption-dependent Mendelian-randomisation evidence, while nicotine trials have not demonstrated clinical benefit. Alcohol findings vary between prospective cohorts, pooled observational analyses and genetic studies. These associations do not justify starting smoking or alcohol for prevention, or prescribing nicotine for PD progression. Key uncertainties include reverse causation, confounding, exposure definitions, genotype subgroup replication and whether any intervention before diagnosis changes incidence.

narrative.documentConcept: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
narrative.text: The 2026 UK Biobank analysis reported no overall coffee–PD association in 435,551 participants with 3319 incident cases, whereas EPIC4PD reported an inverse association. The UK analysis reported differing associations by CYP1A2 genotype; these study-specific results should not be collapsed into a universal protective coffee effect.

narrative.documentConcept: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
narrative.text: Alcohol–PD findings disagree across study designs and reference groups: NeuroEPIC4PD reported no overall baseline or lifetime alcohol association, whereas the 2026 systematic review reported inverse associations in several pooled observational comparisons and inconsistent MR evidence. Neither result establishes that starting alcohol prevents PD.

narrative.documentConcept: Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
narrative.text: EPIC4PD reported an inverse overall coffee association; the 2026 UK Biobank study reported no overall association and genotype-dependent differences. Different cohorts and exposure structures limit direct comparison.

narrative.documentConcept: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
narrative.text: Care partners provide emotional and practical support in PD while facing risks to their own health, social lives and finances. Evidence supports assessing their needs separately, providing tailored information, and arranging practical help, time away and suitable peer support. Neuropsychiatric difficulties, functional impact and caregiver mental health are relevant to burden, but predictors vary by study method. Small psychological and educational studies report benefits in selected domains; pooled findings and other outcomes are less consistent. Resource recommendations should therefore be distinguished from proven treatment effects, and care plans tailored to the relationship and available support.

narrative.documentConcept: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
narrative.text: CBT evidence for care-partner burden is mixed: the preliminary Secker–Brown trial reported improvement, whereas a 2024 meta-analysis reported no significant pooled burden reduction. The positive small trial does not establish a reliable general effect, and the pooled null result does not prove that no individual can benefit.

narrative.documentConcept: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
narrative.text: Evidence on cognition requires qualification: the scoping review described cognitive impairment as a consistent burden predictor, while the 2025 review restricted to multivariable analyses found general cognitive function did not predict burden. These differently scoped findings should remain attributed rather than collapsed into a universal cognitive-score rule.

narrative.documentConcept: Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
narrative.text: A 2024 review reports higher burden with longer disease duration and greater severity; Lesley et al. (2025) find duration, stage and motor severity inconclusive as predictors. This reflects differently scoped syntheses and should be retained as an attributed disagreement.

narrative.documentConcept: CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
narrative.text: PD-adapted CBT addresses mood and anxiety through cognitive and behavioral coping skills. A randomized trial supports telephone CBT added to usual care for depression, while an anxiety trial had different results on its primary and PD-specific secondary measures. Mindfulness yoga and meditation trials suggest mood benefits in selected people with mild-to-moderate PD, but broader anxiety evidence has very low certainty. Cognitive training targets cognitive performance: selected short-term test gains coexist with negative primary and long-term trial outcomes. These studies do not establish dementia prevention. Findings depend on population, comparator, training format and outcome measure.

narrative.documentConcept: Diet and nutrition in PD: Mediterranean, MIND, protein redistribution, ketogenic
narrative.text: Mediterranean and MIND patterns are plausible supportive dietary approaches in Parkinson’s disease, but observational associations cannot establish slower progression. A small Mediterranean trial reported short-term cognitive-test improvements. Protein redistribution may help levodopa-related motor fluctuations, with nutritional and dyskinesia monitoring. Ketogenic pilots suggest possible nonmotor benefits, without established motor superiority or long-term safety. Nutritional adequacy and individualized medication–meal planning remain practical priorities; protocol publications and preliminary associations must not be presented as proven disease modification.

narrative.documentConcept: Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
narrative.text: PD fall prevention combines assessment of gait, balance and orthostatic symptoms with individualized exercise, home-safety assessment and mobility-aid selection. Exercise evidence is strongest for mild-to-moderate PD; improvements in balance or freezing do not invariably translate into fewer falls. Home guidance emphasizes clear routes, lighting, grab bars, seated bathing and emergency communication. Rollator findings are promising but observational, and walking aids can worsen some gait outcomes. Professional assessment should account for cognition, device handling and the home environment. User reports provide practical questions rather than efficacy estimates.

narrative.documentConcept: Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
narrative.text: Living well with PD includes individualized decisions about driving and employment, practical preparation for travel, and adapting personally important daily activities. The Parkinson’s Foundation recommends assessing driving in light of symptoms and medication effects, considering workplace adaptations, and planning medication access and rest when traveling. Occupational therapy offers personalized task and routine strategies. A randomized trial supports improvement in self-perceived daily activity performance, while driving research cautions against equating simulator or test impairment with proven increases in real-world crashes. Patient stories illustrate practical barriers but do not establish universal solutions.

narrative.documentConcept: Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
narrative.text: Multidisciplinary PD care combines professionals around individual symptoms and needs. Some specialist-team models improve quality of life, but rehabilitation comparisons show inconsistent superiority. Virtual specialist visits can reduce travel and improve convenience without reliably improving clinical outcomes. Remote examinations have limits, and digital exclusion can disproportionately affect people with more advanced PD. Recent reviews favor carefully evaluated hybrid care and warn that additional clinical attention can confound comparisons between delivery modes. Evidence should distinguish access, patient experience, clinical effectiveness, and efficiency; it should also retain each study’s intervention, comparator, and population.

narrative.documentConcept: Palliative and advance care planning in PD
narrative.text: Palliative care in PD supports quality of life, symptom relief and planning throughout illness. ACP addresses values, future treatment preferences, surrogate decision-making and documentation. NICE recommends opportunities for prognosis discussions and considering palliative referral at any stage. Trial results depend on the intervention: a 2020 outpatient palliative-care trial improved quality of life and advance-directive completion, while the 2026 PD_Pal trial did not improve its primary documentation endpoint. Early, repeated conversations should account for readiness and possible future cognitive or communication difficulties. The claims below distinguish guideline recommendations, qualitative findings and trial-specific outcomes.
